blocks.x: COM SKILLS 157 · Communication Skills · Topic 6

A grammatically sound sentence needs more than a capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end — it needs a subject, a verb, and a complete thought, and it needs to stay consistent in structure and point of view. This topic trains you to spot and correct the four errors that break these rules: sentence fragments, run-on sentences, faulty parallelism, and shift constructions.

4common types of sentence fragment — dependent-word, −ing, added-details and missing-subject 2types of run-on sentence — fused sentences and comma splices — corrected in 4 standard ways 5kinds of shift construction that break consistency — person, number, tense, voice and mood
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Identify fragment sentences in a piece of English writing, and explain exactly why each one fails to express a complete thought.
2Recognize comma splices, run-on (fused) sentences, and faulty/parallel structures when you meet them in a text.
3Distinguish the two types of run-on sentence — fused sentences and comma splices — and apply all four correction methods to fix either one.
4Avoid fragment sentences, comma splices, and run-on sentences in your own writing, correcting each using the standard techniques.
5Identify the five kinds of shift construction — in person, number, tense, voice and mood — and revise sentences so that they stay consistent throughout.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Sentence Fragment A group of words — a phrase or a dependent clause — that is punctuated like a sentence (capital letter, full stop) but does not express a complete thought or idea. It is an error that occurs when an incomplete sentence is punctuated as though it were complete. Every true sentence needs a subject, a verb, and a complete thought; a fragment is missing at least one of these.

Run-on Sentence An error that occurs when two or more independent clauses are joined without the appropriate punctuation or the use of a correct conjunction. A run-on consists of two complete thoughts running together without any adequate signal to mark the break between them.

Faulty Parallelism & Shift Constructions Parallelism means items in a series must share the same grammatical category, form and function (e.g. all nouns, all −ing forms, all active-voice clauses). Faulty parallelism occurs when the items differ in form or function. A shift construction is a form of faulty parallelism — a sudden, unexpected change in point of view, verb tense, voice, or level of diction across a passage that confuses the reader.
Sentence Fragments→ Run-on Sentences→ Parallelism & Shift Constructions
Incomplete thoughts
A sentence fragment looks like a sentence — it starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop — but something essential is missing: a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.
What is a sentence fragment?

Sentence fragment A group of words — a phrase or a dependent clause — that is punctuated like a sentence but does not express a complete thought or idea. Every sentence must have a subject and a verb, and it must express a complete thought. A word group that lacks a subject, lacks a verb, or fails to express a complete thought is a fragment.
Here are some fragments on their own — read each one and notice that it leaves you waiting for the rest of the thought:

c: Whenever I am waiting for an important phone call.
At the end of the movie, when the battle began.
Although I had never played soccer before.

blocks.x: Four common types of fragment
Dependent-word fragment

Some word groups that begin with a dependent word (a subordinating word such as after, until, when, although, because) are fragments if left cut off from an independent clause. Be careful when you start a sentence with a dependent word.
Fragment: After I cashed my paycheck. I treated myself to dinner.
Revised: After I cashed my paycheck, I treated myself to dinner.
Fragment: I won't leave the house. Until I hear from you.
Revised: I won't leave the house until I hear from you. / Until I hear from you, I won't leave the house.
−ing fragment
When an −ing word appears at or near the start of a word group, a fragment may result, because such a group often lacks a subject and part of the verb needed to stand alone.
Fragment: Boatemaa walked all over the neighbourhood yesterday. Trying to find her dog.
Revised: Boatemaa walked all over the neighbourhood yesterday trying to find her dog.
Added-details fragment
An added-details fragment lacks a subject and verb. It often begins with one of these words: also, especially, like, including, except, for example, such as.
Fragment: Before a race, I eat starchy foods. Such as bread and spaghetti. The carbohydrates provide quick energy.
Revised: Before a race, I eat starchy foods such as bread and spaghetti. The carbohydrates provide quick energy.
Missing-subject fragment
This fragment happens when a clause that shares its subject with the sentence before it is cut off and punctuated on its own — dropping the subject it needs to stand alone.
Fragment: Akosua loved getting wedding presents. But hated writing thank-you notes.
Revised: Akosua loved getting wedding presents but hated writing thank-you notes. / Akosua loved getting wedding presents but she hated writing thank-you notes.
Correcting fragment sentences

items: 1Check for a subject and a verb. The dog in the pet store window. (Fragment) → The dog in the pet store window has eaten. / The dog is in the pet store window. (Revised)

2Remember an −ing verb cannot stand alone as the main verb of a sentence. Your sister having all the skills required of a good salesperson. (Fragment) → Your sister, having all the skills required of a good salesperson, will be appointed. / Your sister has all the skills required of a good salesperson. (Revised)

3A group beginning with also, especially, for example, in addition, moreover, furthermore, etc. needs its own subject and verb. The group is vibrant. Especially the youngest member of the group. (Fragment) → The group is vibrant, especially the youngest member of the group. (Revised)

4A phrase left standing alone is a phrase fragment — supply the missing elements. will soon be sleeping. / inside the house. (Fragments) → The baby will soon be sleeping. / The missing necklace was found inside the house. (Revised)

5A subordinate clause left standing alone is a subordinate-clause fragment — join it to an independent clause. After the candidates arrive. (Fragment) → After the candidates arrive, the inter-halls debate will begin. (Revised)

blocks.title: Quick self-check: fragment or complete sentence?

items: When I want to brighten up my day, I buy a bunch of colorful flowers. Such as carnations or daisies. → the second word group is an added-details fragment — join it: … a bunch of colorful flowers, such as carnations or daisies.

If I can finish writing my paper tonight. I can go to the gym with you tomorrow. → the first word group is a dependent-word fragment — join it: If I can finish writing my paper tonight, I can go to the gym with you tomorrow.
Kofi bought the book and paid for it. → complete sentence — has a subject (Kofi), a verb, and expresses a complete thought.

blocks.x: Two thoughts, one sentence
A run-on sentence crams two or more complete thoughts together without the punctuation or conjunction needed to separate them, so the reader cannot tell where one idea ends and the next begins.
What is a run-on sentence?

Run-on sentence A run-on sentence occurs when two or more independent clauses are joined without the appropriate punctuation or the use of the correct conjunction. Run-on sentences consist of two complete thoughts running together without adequate punctuation to signal the break between them.
Four run-on sentences

c: The bus stopped suddenly I found myself in an old man's lap.
We heard the noise in the garage two birds had flown in through the open window.
Akosua cleans her kitchen every week she shines every pot and pan.
I studied for the test all weekend I am well prepared for it.

blocks.x: Two types of run-on sentence
Fused sentence

A fused sentence has no punctuation at all marking the break between the two independent clauses — the clauses are simply fused together. Example: The bus stopped suddenly I found myself in an old man's lap.
Comma splice

A comma splice is an error that occurs when you punctuate the break between two independent clauses with a comma instead of a period or a semicolon. Example: The bus stopped suddenly, I found myself in an old man's lap.
Four ways to correct a run-on sentence
Here is the same run-on — The bus stopped suddenly I found myself in an old man's lap. — corrected using each of the four standard methods:

items: 1Use a period and a capital letter to separate the two sentences. The bus stopped suddenly. I found myself in an old man's lap.
2Use a comma and a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS — for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). The bus stopped suddenly, and I found myself in an old man's lap.
3Use a semicolon to connect the two thoughts. The bus stopped suddenly; I found myself in an old man's lap.
4Use a subordinating conjunction to join the two thoughts into one main idea and one dependent idea. When the bus stopped suddenly, I found myself in an old man's lap.

blocks.title: Apply all four fixes to another run-on

blocks.x: Original run-on: Akosua cleans her kitchen every week she shines every pot and pan.

items: Period + capital: Akosua cleans her kitchen every week. She shines every pot and pan.
Comma + FANBOYS: Akosua cleans her kitchen every week, and she shines every pot and pan.
Semicolon: Akosua cleans her kitchen every week; she shines every pot and pan.
Subordinating conjunction: When Akosua cleans her kitchen every week, she shines every pot and pan.

blocks.x: Balance and consistency

Good sentences keep items in a series in matching grammatical form, and keep point of view, tense, voice and mood consistent across a passage. When either of these breaks down, the result is faulty parallelism or a shift construction.
What is parallelism?

Parallelism Parallelism means that items arranged in a series must be parallel or balanced — of the same grammatical category (noun, verb, etc.), the same grammatical form (number: singular/plural; aspect: progressive/perfective; voice: active/passive), and must perform the same grammatical function.
Parallel (correct)
Dancing, singing and writing are my hobbies. — all three items are −ing (gerund) forms.
To dance, to sing and to write are my hobbies. — all three items are infinitive (to + verb) forms.
Faulty parallelism
Of all the sports I've played, I prefer tennis, handball, and playing golf. — mixes two nouns (tennis, handball) with a −ing phrase (playing golf). Revised: … I prefer tennis, handball, and golf.
He is a good choice for manager because he works hard, he keeps calm and well-liked. — mixes two clauses with an adjective. Revised: … because he works hard, keeps calm, and is well-liked.
What is a shift construction?

Shift construction A shift construction is an example of faulty parallelism: a sudden, unexpected change in point of view, verb tense, voice, or level of diction that may confuse your readers. Shifts most often occur across a paragraph, not just inside one sentence — so consistency has to be maintained sentence after sentence.
Shift in Person→ Shift in Number→ Shift in Tense→ Shift in Voice→ Shift in Mood
Shift in person

Person Person distinguishes the person talking (first person: I, we), the person spoken to (second person: you), and the person, object or concept being talked about (third person: he, she, they, one, a person, people). Most shifts in person happen when a writer mixes the generic third person (a person, one, people, they) with the second person (you) while referring to people in general.
Shift: If a person works hard, you can gain recognition.
Revised: If you work hard, you can gain recognition. (consistent second person)
Revised: If a person works hard, he or she can gain recognition. (consistent third person singular)
Better: If people work hard, they can gain recognition. (third person plural — the most natural of the three)

Note that each of these on its own is acceptable — People should not drive when they have been drinking., One should not drive when he or she has been drinking., and You should not drive when you have been drinking. all share the same meaning from a different point of view. The error is only in mixing them within the same sentence or passage.
Shift in number

Number
Number refers to the distinction between one (singular) and more than one (plural). Inconsistency in number occurs most often between a pronoun and its antecedent.
Shift: If a student does not understand a lesson, they should consult the instructor. (singular antecedent "a student" — plural pronoun "they")
Revised: If students do not understand a lesson, they should consult the instructor. (both plural)
Revised: A student who does not understand a lesson should consult the instructor. (rewritten to avoid the pronoun mismatch entirely)
Shift in tense

Tense
Maintain consistency in verb tense throughout a sentence, paragraph or essay, unless the meaning genuinely requires a change of tense. Changes not required by meaning distract the reader.
Shift: The virus mutated so quickly that it develops a resistance to most vaccines. (past → present)
Revised: The virus mutates so quickly that it develops a resistance to most vaccines. (present throughout)
Shift: The city's crime rate continues to decrease, but experts disagreed on the reasons. (present → past)
Revised: The city's crime rate continues to decrease, but experts disagree on the reasons. (present throughout)
Shift in voice

Voice In the active voice, the subject is the actor performing the action of the verb; in the passive voice, the subject is acted upon. Unnecessary shifts between active and passive voice can disorient readers and create confusion.
Shift: Internet newsgroups cover an enormous range of topics for discussion. Forums for meeting people with like interests are provided in these groups. (active → passive)
Revised: Internet newsgroups cover an enormous range of topics for discussion and provide forums for meeting people with like interests. (active throughout)
Shift: Drought and windstorms made farming impossible and many families were forced to leave Okom village due to starvation. (active → passive)
Revised: Drought and windstorms made farming impossible, and starvation forced many families to leave Okom village. (active throughout)
Shift in mood

Mood Mood indicates whether a sentence states a fact or asks a question (indicative mood), gives a command or direction (imperative mood), or expresses a condition or suggestion (subjunctive mood). Shifts in mood occur most frequently in directions, when a writer moves back and forth between the imperative and the indicative.
Shift: Cook the mixture slowly, and you should stir it until the sugar is dissolved. (imperative → indicative)
Revised: Cook the mixture slowly and stir it until the sugar is dissolved. (imperative throughout)

items: A bank commonly owes more to its customers than is held in reserve. → shift in voice (passive "is held" instead of active "it holds").
Then demand will exceed supplies, and banks failed. → shift in tense (future "will exceed" then past "failed").
These days, a person's losses are not likely to be great because the government insures your deposits. → shift in person ("a person" then "your").
